text: IB Course Results (certificates rather than a full diploma) need at least 18 points, grade 3 or above in all six subjects, at least 3 subjects at Higher Level, and at least one subject at Danish A level and one at Danish B level.
AAU publishes a conversion chart showing which IB subjects and levels count as Danish A, B or C levels.

AAU lists exactly five bachelor's degrees for international students. Four are taught in English and are listed here. The fifth, Language and International Studies, English (Aalborg), is listed on the same page but its own programme page states the language of instruction is Danish and requires Danish A, so it is not included.

Academic year 2026 (two semesters): DKK 115,700 for BSc Applied Industrial Electronics, BSc Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology and BSc Energy Engineering; DKK 55,600 for BSc Economics and Business Administration. Application fee EUR 150. EU/EEA students pay nothing.

Mathematics equivalent to a Danish A-level and Physics equivalent to a Danish B-level or Geoscience equivalent to a Danish A-level and Chemistry equivalent to a Danish B-level or Biotechnology equivalent to a Danish A-level and English equivalent to Danish B-level.

Engineering for biotechnological production: using cells and microorganisms to make medicines, food and fuels, and to treat waste water. It is taught in Kalundborg with Novo Nordisk, Novonesis and Lundbeck nearby, and includes a five-month internship. Needs Maths A, Physics B, Chemistry B and English B, and every quota 2 applicant is interviewed.
With passed: Mathematics equivalent to a Danish A-level and Physics equivalent to a Danish B-level or Geoscience equivalent to a Danish A-level and English equivalent to Danish B-level.

For the Danish A requirement (which no English-taught programme has, but which matters if you also apply to Danish-taught programmes): Danish/Norwegian/Swedish A or A Literature at HL or SL counts as Danish A, and Danish/Norwegian/Swedish B HL counts as Danish A only in combination with English A. Danish B at SL is not accepted.

AU tells Danish applicants to treat the English-taught Computer Science, Data Science and IT Product Development degrees as the harder route and to apply to the Danish-taught equivalents (Datalogi, Datavidenskab, It-produktudvikling) as well. For Data Science AU says outright that the English version "is intended for international students". The two versions lead to the same English-taught master's.
AU advises Danish applicants to also apply for the Danish-taught Datalogi, because the English-taught programme has limited spots.

AU: "The international Bachelor's Degree Programme in Data Science has limited spots and is intended for international students. Applicants with Danish A are therefore advised to apply for the corresponding Danish-taught programme in Datavidenskab as their first priority."
AU advises Danish applicants to also apply for the Danish-taught It-Produktudvikling.

Academic year 2026/2027, per year (60 ECTS): EUR 13,000 for Cognitive Science and for Economics and Business Administration in both Aarhus and Herning; EUR 17,300 for Computer Science, Data Science and IT Product Development. Application fee EUR 150 (DKK 1,125) per applicant, payable by 15 March and refunded only if you enrol and are still enrolled on 1 October. AU states: "Aarhus University does not offer scholarships for any of our Bachelor's degree programmes." EU/EEA and Swiss citizens pay nothing.

The broad business economics degree — strategy, finance, marketing, organisation — with everything framed around companies operating across borders. About half the compulsory courses use mathematics as a working tool, at roughly the level of the entry requirement. It is the most applied-to and the highest cut-off of any CBS bachelor, and a third of the students are non-Danish.

A small, highly structured degree about the industry that moves physical goods: shipping markets, chartering, maritime law, logistics and trade finance. The second year includes a compulsory semester abroad in Singapore, Hong Kong or Greece, and the final year includes a compulsory internship in a shipping company. Only 75 places, and half of them are decided in quota 2.

EUR 6,500 per semester (EUR 13,000 per year), or DKK 49,000 per semester (DKK 98,000 per year), for bachelor programmes. Application fee EUR 150 (approximately DKK 1,125) per applicant per admission round, payable by 15 March at 12.00 CET. EU/EEA and Swiss citizens pay neither.

The Danish-taught undergraduate degrees come in two families: BSc Eng (civilingeniør, a 3-year academic bachelor) and BEng (diplomingeniør, a 3.5-year professional engineering degree, many of them taught at DTU's Ballerup campus). Both require Danish A and are described only on DTU's Danish-language site, so they are not listed here.

A broad engineering degree that starts with heavy maths, physics and chemistry and then narrows into one of four specialisations: Living Systems, Advanced Materials, Cyber Systems or Future Energy. Year one introduces at least two of the specialisations through design-build projects, and the third year leaves room for a semester abroad or an industry project. About 60 per cent of the students are international, so it suits you if you want an engineering degree in English without having to pick your exact branch at 17.

ITU offers four bachelor's degrees but only two are taught in English. BSc Software Development is taught in Danish and requires Danish A; BSc Digital Design and Interactive Technologies is mainly Danish (only the second year is taught entirely in English) and also requires Danish A. Neither is listed here.

A qualifying examination certificate equal to a Danish upper secondary school leaving certificate. Mathematics corresponding to the Danish A-level with an average mark of at least 6. English corresponding to the Danish B-level with an average mark of at least 6 (no grade requirement if you have passed English at Danish A-level).
Danish A must be passed even though teaching is in English.

A qualifying examination certificate that can be equated with a Danish upper secondary school leaving certificate. Mathematics corresponding to the Danish B-level with an average mark of at least 6. English corresponding to the Danish B-level with an average mark of at least 6. Danish at A level is a requirement. No required mark but the subject must be passed. You must be proficient in oral and written English, as the programme is taught in English. There is no grade requirement in Mathematics or English if you passed the subject at Danish A level.
EUR 200 (DKK 1,490). Refunded only if you are admitted and registered as an active student on 1 September of the year of admission.

English at Danish B-level. Mathematics at Danish A-level. One of the following combinations: Physics B and Chemistry B; Physics B and Biotechnology A; Chemistry B and Geoscience A; or Chemistry B and Biology A and Physics C.
The second foreign language must be at Danish B level if it is a continued language, or Danish A level if you began it from scratch; it cannot be English or your school's language of instruction.

English at Danish B-level. History or History of Ideas or Contemporary History at Danish B-level. One additional language — either a beginner's language at Danish A-level or an advanced language at Danish B-level. The additional language cannot be English or the language of instruction of your upper secondary education.

Sønderborg holds eleven of SDU's fifteen fully English-taught bachelor's degrees. It is a small town on the island of Als in the far south of Jutland, closer to Flensburg in Germany than to any large Danish city, and several hours from Copenhagen by train. The campus, Alsion, is a single modern building shared with a concert hall, and the student body there is strongly international — partly because Danish applicants mostly do not move that far south. Mads Clausen's company Danfoss is based next door, which is why so much of the engineering sits here.

Vejle is SDU's newest campus and holds four English-taught degrees, all of them IT. SDU calls it "Denmark's newest IT campus". Vejle is a mid-sized town on the east coast of Jutland on the main motorway and rail line, with a cluster of IT employers nearby, so student jobs are realistic.

Odense is SDU's headquarters and Denmark's third-largest city, half an hour from Copenhagen by fast train — but only one fully English-taught bachelor's degree is taught there, Market and Management Anthropology. If you want Odense and you do not speak Danish, your options are almost nil at bachelor level.

Hands-on electronics engineering: analogue and digital circuits, signal processing, high-frequency technology and electric motors, with semester projects such as smart homes, motor testing and drone control. Mathematics is heavy in the first part. The sixth semester is a six-month internship in Denmark or abroad.
Compulsory fieldwork abroad in a country of your choice.

Anthropology used as a business tool: fieldwork, cross-cultural analysis and the study of how people actually behave as consumers, combined with management. It includes a compulsory period of fieldwork abroad in a country you choose. SDU runs it as a "signature programme" — a small intake with intense teaching and frequent feedback — and it is the only fully English-taught bachelor's degree on the Odense campus.

Studieprøven has four parts — oral, listening, reading and written — and "must be passed with at least grade 02 in each of all the 3 examination disciplines". Medicine, Dentistry and Dental Hygiene require grade 7 rather than 02 in each discipline. Alternatively you can pass a supplementary upper secondary course in Danish A.

If you genuinely want UCPH at bachelor level, the route is Danish. Either take Danish A as your IB Language A or B HL subject, or plan to pass Studieprøven i dansk som andetsprog. Studieprøven is normally reached after roughly two to three years of Danish courses, so this is a decision to take in the first year of the Diploma Programme at the latest.

Each VIA programme page says every specific subject must be passed with a minimum average of 2.0 on the Danish scale. Applicants with non-Danish qualifications are asked for a verification form, stamped by their school, that confirms the hours taught in each required subject over the last three years.

Mathematics equivalent to a Danish A-level. Physics equivalent to a Danish B-level or Geoscience equivalent to a Danish A-level. Chemistry equivalent to a Danish C-level or Biotechnology equivalent to a Danish A-level. English equivalent to a Danish B-level. [...] Each of the subjects above must be passed with a min. average of 2.0 on the Danish grading scale.

Mathematics equivalent to a Danish B-level (applicants with Danish Admission course for engineering programmes are required to have Mathematics at an A-level). English equivalent to a Danish A-level. [...] Each of the subjects above must be passed with a min. average of 2.0 on the Danish grading scale.

Mathematics equivalent to a Danish A-level. English equivalent to a Danish B-level. Physics equivalent to a Danish B-level or Geoscience equivalent to a Danish A-level. Chemistry equivalent to a Danish C-level or Biotechnology equivalent to a Danish A-level. [...] Each of the subjects above must be passed with a min. average of 2.0 on the Danish grading scale.

Mathematics equivalent to a Danish A-level. Physics equivalent to a Danish B-level or Geoscience equivalent to a Danish A-level. English equivalent to a Danish B-level. [...] Each of the subjects above must be passed with a min. average of 2.0 on the Danish grading scale.

Architectural Technology and Construction Management (Horsens): a 3.5-year, 210 ECTS bachelor with August and February starts, admitting IB holders with Mathematics at C level (passed with at least 2.0), and selecting in quota 2 on a motivational video, grades, work experience and stays abroad.

Zealand's admission page for its English-taught degrees gives the same subject requirements. For ATCM, English B or an accepted test (IELTS Academic 6.5 and others). It ranks applicants on grade average, other education, work, time abroad and higher subject levels, and sometimes interviews. Non-EU applicants pay a EUR 300 application fee.
The Danish Agency republishes its IB conversion table by 1 March each year for that summer's intake. Re-verify every March.
Grant rates are set annually and eligibility rules change. Danish SU changes on 1 January 2027 for this cohort.
Danish A1 HL / Danish A Literature HL — meets Danish A.
Danish A1 SL / Danish A Literature SL — normally accepted for Danish A at university, because it sits above the Studieprøven test.
Studieprøven i dansk — the national Danish language test for higher education. Universities may allow it in place of Danish A for applicants with a non-Nordic qualification.
Danish A Literature HL (from 2013)
Danish A Literature SL (from 2013)
Danish A1 SL / A Literature SL is normally accepted as meeting a Danish A entry requirement at university, because it sits above the Studieprøven language test.

Danish ab initio, Danish B HL and Danish B SL are foreign-language subjects aimed at listening, speaking, reading and writing Danish. Whether Danish ab initio or Danish B HL can replace Danish A as the Danish-language requirement is left to each institution.

The IB Diploma Programme subject catalogue, and nothing else. One entry per real IB subject with the levels it is offered at. This file used to carry a second, unnamed table saying what each subject counts as in Denmark; that table is now data/recognition/dk.json, because it was never a property of the IB subject — it was one country reading the IB subject. A requirement written in IB terms needs only this file.

Danish A: Language and Literature

Non-EU tuition at institution level: Academic year 2026 (two semesters): DKK 115,700 for BSc Applied Industrial Electronics, BSc Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology and BSc Energy Engineering; DKK 55,600 for BSc Economics and Business Administration. Application fee EUR 150. EU/EEA students pay nothing.

Non-EU tuition at institution level: Academic year 2026/2027, per year (60 ECTS): EUR 13,000 for Cognitive Science and for Economics and Business Administration in both Aarhus and Herning; EUR 17,300 for Computer Science, Data Science and IT Product Development. Application fee EUR 150 (DKK 1,125) per applicant, payable by 15 March and refunded only if you enrol and are still enrolled on 1 October. AU states: "Aarhus University does not offer scholarships for any of our Bachelor's degree programmes." EU/EEA and Swiss citizens pay nothing.

Non-EU tuition at institution level: EUR 6,500 per semester (EUR 13,000 per year), or DKK 49,000 per semester (DKK 98,000 per year), for bachelor programmes. Application fee EUR 150 (approximately DKK 1,125) per applicant per admission round, payable by 15 March at 12.00 CET. EU/EEA and Swiss citizens pay neither.
Every student also pays a material fee each semester: DKK 2,678 for ceramics and DKK 3,346 for glass in autumn 2026. The 2027 fees will be published in March 2027.
One additional language – either beginner’s language at Danish A-level or advanced language at Danish B-level

Applications received by 15 March are assessed on a motivational video, upper-secondary exam results, work experience (at least 30 hours a week for three months), stays abroad of at least three months and relevant courses of at least six months.

Applicants are ranked on the grade average of their qualifying exam, other relevant higher education, at least three months of relevant work, at least three months of study abroad, volunteering or military service, and required subjects passed at a higher level than required.

A Selection Factor and not a requirement: BUas says the level "will be discussed" in the interview and sets no threshold. For a Danish IB student taking a Group 2 language this is worth raising unprompted.

Denmark lets you top up a missing level through gymnasial supplering, taken at a VUC or GSK centre. Two things to know before you plan around it: the courses are taught in Danish, and GSK can only meet a specific subject requirement — it cannot raise your overall qualification level.

If you hold a full IB Diploma your qualification level is already fine, so GSK is exactly the right tool for a missing Mathematics A. If you hold DP Course Results rather than a Diploma, GSK is the wrong tool entirely. Your qualification level is not yet university-bachelor standard, and the Agency says plainly that GSK cannot raise it — that takes hf-enkeltfag, or sitting the subjects as a self-study candidate. Taking a GSK course in that situation costs you a term and changes nothing. GSK is still the right tool for a specific subject requirement at an erhvervsakademi or professionsbachelor programme, and a subject taken for that stays valid if you later switch to a university bachelor.

Free tuition and an expensive city can easily cost more than modest tuition somewhere cheap. Norway charges no tuition and budgets NOK 15,488 a month to live. Copenhagen is the most expensive place to be a student in Denmark by a distance, and several strong English-taught programmes are in cities that cost half as much.

If you are a Danish citizen, work out early whether SU follows you. It does, for a full degree abroad. In another Nordic country you get SU and loans exactly as if you studied in Denmark — which, for anyone starting from 2025, means the prescribed length of the programme and no more. Elsewhere, at most four years (48 klip).

Everything on this site is a description. Sønderborg and Copenhagen are both in Denmark and are not remotely the same experience, and no amount of careful prose substitutes for standing in a place for an afternoon.

Open days are the obvious route. Failing that, a train ticket and a wander is cheap compared to three years somewhere you did not want to be.
Decide whether you need Danish at A level

Most Danish bachelor's degrees are taught in Danish and require Danish at A level. If you took Danish A1 or Danish A Literature at either level you already have it. If you did not, and you want a Danish-taught programme, you will need Studieprøven i dansk or an equivalent.

This is the single biggest constraint on studying in Denmark with an IB, and it is rarely stated as a headline. The University of Copenhagen teaches every one of its bachelor's degrees in Danish.

Danish applications close on 15 March and IB results are not released until 6 July. The mechanism that resolves this is the IB's own results service: your coordinator registers you and your results travel directly to up to six institutions.

Get a receipt. This is administrative rather than academic, and it is the single most common way an otherwise complete application fails.

Tests are required rather than optional wherever they appear, and their registration deadlines sit well before the application deadlines — UAT-UK for Oxford and Cambridge closes in late September, two and a half weeks before the UCAS deadline in mid-October. Austria's MedAT registration closes in March for a July test, roughly a year before results.

SDU in Denmark uses the uniTEST for quota 2. Italy uses TOLC and IMAT. Central European medical schools run their own entrance exams, several of which can be sat online from Denmark.

Copenhagen Business School requires one on all six of its English-taught programmes. The Dutch numerus fixus selection procedures usually include something similar. US applications are built around it.

One sharp caveat for a May 2027 IB candidate applying to CBS: its essay only counts in the Danish quota 2 round if at least three months have passed since you finished school. If you apply straight from the IB, your essay does not count. That is the kind of rule that makes the difference between a considered application and a wasted one.

Many Danish institutions count documented relevant work or education in quota 2 — Aalborg, for example, counts up to twelve months. The documentation has to be specific: an employer's statement giving your responsibilities, the period of employment, weekly hours and a signature.

Aalborg is refreshingly blunt that motivational letters and recommendations are *not* considered relevant in its quota 2 and are not required. Other institutions differ. Check the one you want rather than assuming.

In systems with holistic admissions — the US most of all, and UK personal statements to a lesser degree — sustained depth in one or two things reads far better than a long list. Admissions officers read thousands of these and can tell the difference between a commitment and a collection.

In most of Europe this has no effect whatsoever. Danish quota 1 is grades alone, and quota 2 counts documented work rather than interests. Do not build an activity portfolio for a European application; it will not be read.

CAS is required by the IB and by essentially no university. No admissions office in Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Germany or the Netherlands will read it. Treating it as an admissions instrument is a misunderstanding that costs students a lot of stress for nothing.

What it is genuinely good for: finding out whether you like something before you commit three years to it. A student who volunteers in a hospital and discovers they cannot stand it has learned something far more valuable than a line on a form. That is worth doing deliberately.
Formally Danish A1 SL maps to Danish B, but universities normally accept it for a Danish A requirement because it sits above the Studieprøven test.
Danish B is a foreign-language subject. Whether it can replace Danish A as the language requirement is decided by each institution — ask in writing.

Most of this site is organised by country, because most students choose a country first. This page is for the routes that do not fit that shape — degrees spread across several cities, joint degrees run by alliances of universities, tiny liberal-arts colleges inside big systems, professional schools that train you for one industry, and the Danish habit of not starting university straight away. Everything listed here was checked in September 2026 and is operating for a 2027 start. Two things you may have read about elsewhere are deliberately absent: Yale-NUS College in Singapore has closed and no longer admits students, and Quest University Canada is not currently admitting either — its site now says it is combining with Columbia College into a new British Columbia university, with programmes and admission requirements still being prepared. Where we could not verify a fee or a deadline from an official page, the field says so rather than guessing.

Someone who found the IB's breadth and its emphasis on how you know things genuinely interesting rather than an obstacle, who is comfortable being uprooted every year, and who does not need a campus, a sports club or a student bar to feel at home. It is a poor fit if you want a lab, a workshop or a studio.

SIMAC and MARTEC are Danish public institutions, so tuition is free for EU/EEA citizens and Danish SU applies. Swedish and British academies charge according to their national systems. Individual figures not verified.

Danish maritime academies recruit through the standard Danish admission system (optagelse.dk) with the usual 15 March and 5 July deadlines. Sea-time placements are arranged through the academy and shipping companies.

A route almost invisible from a gymnasium, and one of the few where a bachelor's degree comes with a licence attached. Maritime academies train ship's officers and marine engineers: SIMAC in Svendborg and MARTEC in Frederikshavn in Denmark, Chalmers and Linnaeus University in Sweden, Warsash Maritime School in Southampton. Degrees combine classroom study with long periods of sea time on commercial vessels, and the qualification is a Certificate of Competency recognised internationally under the STCW convention as well as an academic degree.
Svendborg and Frederikshavn in Denmark; Gothenburg, Kalmar and Chalmers in Sweden; Southampton and Warsash in the UK

Someone who wants a degree that leads directly to a licensed profession, who is comfortable with long periods away from home, and who wants to work at sea for some years before coming ashore into shipping, offshore wind, surveying or port management. Denmark, with Maersk and one of the world's largest merchant fleets, is an unusually good place to hold this qualification.

Integrated ATPL training in Europe is typically a large six-figure DKK sum, self-financed. University aviation degrees follow ordinary national tuition rules. No figures were verified in this research.
Charged per week, with the state covering a substantial share for Danish students. Prices were not readable from the association's site — see the prices page at danishfolkhighschools.com.
Danish højskoler and the sabbatår

Almost everyone, and this is the part foreign admissions officers do not understand: taking a sabbatår is the Danish norm, not a sign of drift. Most Danish students take one or two years between gymnasium and university, and the system is built to expect it. For the destinations in this dataset, a sabbatår has a specific advantage — several Asian universities run March or April intakes, and several Western universities in Asia have deadlines that fall before your IB results. A gap year converts that from a problem into a choice.

Sciences Po charges income-scaled tuition for EU students, which for lower-income families can be zero. Partner-university fees apply for the years abroad and can be substantial at the American partners. Figures were not verified from an official page.
year abroad

Sciences Po's undergraduate College is a three-year Bachelor of Arts in the humanities and social sciences, taught on one of seven French campuses, each with a regional specialisation: Dijon for central and eastern Europe, Le Havre for Asia-Pacific, Menton for the Mediterranean and Middle East, Nancy for the Franco-German partnership, Poitiers for Latin America, Reims for Africa and North America, and Paris with no regional focus. The third year is compulsorily spent abroad at one of 480 partner universities, sometimes with an internship attached. Alongside this, Sciences Po runs eleven dual bachelor's degrees with universities around the world — two years in France and two at the partner, graduating with both degrees — and has recently added duals with ESCP Business School and with the Columbia Climate School on ecological transition and climate risks. Eighteen dual-degree programmes exist in total.
Paris, Dijon, Le Havre, Menton, Nancy, Poitiers and Reims — plus a partner university abroad
Sciences Po — Undergraduate College, campuses, year abroad and dual degrees
Danish Folk High Schools (FFD) — English information site

Every year a group of Danish students who do not get a place on medicin at KU, AU, SDU or AAU go and study medicine in English somewhere else in Europe. Poland, Hungary and Czechia are the three countries that take the most of them. It is a real route and it works, but it is expensive and there is one legal detail that decides whether your degree lets you work as a doctor in Denmark. This page explains how entry works, what it costs, and exactly what you have to check before you sign anything.

Whether Denmark accepts a specific non-Polish supervised year in place of the Polish staz podyplomowy could not be verified from an official Danish page; the student must ask Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed directly.
Danish SU and udlandsstipendium rules for six-year medical degrees abroad were not verified from an official Danish source in this pass and must be checked at su.dk / ufm.dk.

Danish medicine places are rationed. If you do not get in, the options are to re-apply, to do something else, or to pay for an English-taught medical degree abroad. Central European universities have run English-language medical programmes for decades, originally for American and Scandinavian students, and they are set up for exactly this. The teaching is in English for the whole degree. The patients are not, so you learn the local language alongside it for the clinical years.

This is a six-year undergraduate-entry degree, the same shape as the Danish one. You start straight after the IB. There is no separate pre-med.
Entry is by entrance exam and interview, not by a Danish grade-point average, so a strong IB student who missed the Danish cut-off is competitive.
Take HL Biology and HL Chemistry if medicine abroad is even a maybe. Almost every entrance exam is built on that content.

Tuition is the big number and it is paid every year for six years. Add living costs on top. See the Poland, Czechia and Hungary country pages on this site for the specific per-university figures and the academic year each one belongs to.

Danish SU and the Danish state student loan (SU-lan) can often be taken abroad for a full degree, and there is a separate scheme for tuition support. That is decided by Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen in Denmark, not by the university abroad, and you have to apply for it yourself. Do that early, because it changes whether the whole plan is affordable.
Living costs in Poland, Czechia and Hungary are well below Danish levels, which offsets part of the tuition.
Check the Danish SU rules for udlandsstipendium and SU abroad before you commit. This is a Danish decision made in Denmark.

A medical degree is not the same thing as a licence to work as a doctor. In Denmark the licence is called autorisation, and the right to work without supervision is called tilladelse til selvstaendigt virke. Both are granted by Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed.

The good news is that EU law is on your side. Under Directive 2005/36/EC on the recognition of professional qualifications, a medical qualification listed in Annex V point 5.1.1 is recognised automatically across the EU. Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed states plainly that you can get Danish authorisation and permission to practise independently if you are a citizen of an EU/EEA country or Switzerland and hold a medical degree from an EU/EEA country or Switzerland. Denmark does not make you repeat the Danish klinisk basisuddannelse in that case, and it does not make you sit a Danish medical exam.

The authority also says that automatic recognition depends on the education, not on the passport: someone who is not an EU citizen but who trained as a doctor in the EU/EEA may still be recognised under the automatic-recognition principles.
Applying for the authorisation itself is free. The permission to practise independently costs DKK 3,689.
The stated processing target is three months from a complete application, with priority given to applicants who already have a Danish job offer.
Automatic recognition covers doctors, dentists, midwives and nurses. It rests on Directive 2005/36/EC and Danish executive order no. 49 of 13 January 2010.
The part that decides everything: Danish authorisation

This is the single most important thing on this page and it is the thing recruitment agencies do not tell you.

Annex V of the Directive lists, for each country, the qualification that gets automatic recognition and any certificates that must accompany it. For Czechia, Hungary and Estonia, the medical diploma stands alone: no accompanying certificate is listed. For Poland it does not. The Polish entry requires the diploma plus the certificate of the state final medical examination, the Lekarski Egzamin Koncowy (LEK), and Poland's own medical chamber says the certificate of completed postgraduate internship, staz podyplomowy, is also part of what accompanies the Polish diploma.

The Naczelna Izba Lekarska, the Polish chamber of physicians, puts it bluntly: it can only certify full Polish qualifications for EU recognition if you have both the LEK and a recognised postgraduate internship. If you have neither, what you can get instead is an Article 23 or 27 certificate of conformity, and the chamber says that certificate does not confirm that a graduate of a Polish university has obtained full qualifications to practise the profession in Poland.

In plain terms: if you graduate in Poland, come straight home and skip the LEK and the internship, you are not in the automatic-recognition track. You can still work towards Danish authorisation, but you are on a slower and less certain path.

Denmark has a fallback for exactly this situation. The regional postgraduate training secretariats run what they call a KBU-lignende forlob, a KBU-like programme, for doctors trained inside the EU, EEA and the Nordic countries who have not been granted automatic authorisation. Doctors trained outside the EU/EEA go through a longer route of evalueringsansaettelser, evaluation posts of at least two times six months.

So the fallback exists, but it costs you time and it depends on getting a post. It is much better to graduate with the full set of documents than to arrive home and negotiate.
KBU itself is two six-month posts, one in a hospital and one usually in general practice or psychiatry, and Danish graduates must register for it within two years of finishing their degree.
A Dane with an EU medical degree that qualifies for automatic recognition does not have to go through KBU to get permission to practise independently.
Rules and fees change. The Danish authorisation fee structure was reworked on 1 July 2024, and restrictions introduced since then have been aimed at non-EU/EEA educations, not EU ones.

There is no formal Danish language test imposed by Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed on doctors trained inside the EU. Under EU law the authority has to issue the authorisation on the basis of the qualification. Danish language competence is treated as the employer's responsibility, and Danish hospitals do check it.

That cuts both ways. Legally you are fine. Practically, a Danish hospital will not hire you if your clinical Danish is weak, and if you have spent six years working in Polish, Hungarian or Czech, your Danish medical vocabulary will be thin. Danish doctors' organisations have publicly argued for a formal language test for EU-trained doctors; that has not become law, but it tells you what employers think.

Keep your Danish alive while you are away. Do Danish-language clinical placements or summer jobs in Denmark if you can.
No Danish language exam is required for authorisation if you trained in the EU/EEA.
The employer is responsible for making sure your Danish is good enough for the job.
You will also need the local language for clinical years abroad, so you are learning two languages at once.
This is a live political debate in Denmark, so check whether the rule has changed by the time you graduate.
What does Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen say about SU and tuition support for this specific programme?
Studying medicine abroad and coming home to practise in Denmark
